questions.q: Define autogamy and give one example of a plant that commonly exhibits it.
questions.a: Autogamy is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma within the same flower. Example: wheat, rice, or pea. A wrong answer (e.g., "transfer between different flowers of the same plant") reveals confusion between autogamy and geitonogamy — the student is focusing on "same plant" rather than "same flower".

questions.q: Why is geitonogamy considered genetically equivalent to autogamy even though it requires a pollinating agent?
questions.a: Geitonogamy involves pollen transfer between different flowers of the same plant. Since all flowers of a plant share the same genotype (barring somatic mutations), the pollen and ovule carry identical alleles. A wrong answer (e.g., "because it uses wind") shows the student confuses the *mechanism* (agent requirement) with the *genetic consequence* (homozygosity).

questions.q: A farmer grows a pure line of tomato (self-pollinated) and a hybrid maize (cross-pollinated) in adjacent fields. If he saves seeds from both for next season, which crop will show greater phenotypic variation in the offspring and why?
questions.a: Maize will show greater variation because it is predominantly xenogamous (cross-pollinated), reshuffling alleles each generation. Tomato is autogamous, so saved seeds remain genetically uniform. A wrong answer (e.g., "tomato because it has more flowers") indicates the student cannot link pollination type to genetic segregation and recombination.

questions.q: Compare the genetic consequences of autogamy, geitonogamy, and xenogamy in a heterozygous plant (Aa). Which type(s) can produce aa homozygous recessive offspring in one generation?
questions.a: Autogamy and geitonogamy (both selfing) can produce aa offspring (1/4 probability) because the same plant provides both gametes. Xenogamy between two Aa plants can also produce aa (1/4), but if the partner is AA, no aa offspring result. A wrong answer (e.g., "only xenogamy produces variation") shows the student thinks cross-pollination is the only source of homozygosity, missing that selfing exposes recessive alleles faster.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Geitonogamy is ecologically cross-pollination but genetically self-pollination." Is it correct? Justify.
questions.a: Correct. Ecologically, geitonogamy requires a vector (insect, wind) to move pollen between flowers — an inter-flower transfer. Genetically, the pollen and ovule originate from the same individual, so allele combinations are identical to autogamy. A wrong evaluation (e.g., "false because it uses an agent") reveals the student equates "cross-pollination" solely with the presence of an agent, ignoring genetic identity.

questions.q: Design a simple field experiment to determine whether a newly discovered flowering plant is predominantly autogamous or xenogamous. List the steps and the expected observations for each case.
questions.a: Steps: (1) Bag several buds before anthesis to exclude pollinators. (2) Leave similar buds unbagged as controls. (3) After flowering, compare fruit/seed set in bagged vs. unbagged flowers. (4) If bagged flowers set seeds equally well → autogamy. (5) If bagged flowers fail but unbagged succeed → xenogamy. A poor design (e.g., "observe insects visiting") shows the student confuses pollinator visitation with actual pollen transfer and fertilization success.
